standards.SEV1: Flow of energy and cycling of matter within an ecosystem
standards.SEV2: Stability and change in Earth's ecosystems
standards.SEV3: Types, availability, allocation, and sustainability of energy resources
standards.SEV5: Effects of human population growth on global ecosystems

elements.SEV1b: Laws of Thermodynamics & energy transfer (food chains/webs, trophic levels, 10% rule)
elements.SEV1c: Biogeochemical cycles (water, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, oxygen)
elements.SEV1d: Physical factors & organismal adaptations in terrestrial biomes
elements.SEV1e: Chemical & physical properties of Georgia aquatic biomes
elements.SEV2a: Short- & long-term natural climate fluctuations (El Niño, volcanism, Milankovitch)
elements.SEV2b: Atmospheric chemistry (CO₂, methane) & the greenhouse effect
elements.SEV2d: Value of biodiversity in ecosystem resilience
elements.SEV3a: Origin & consumption of renewable & non-renewable energy
elements.SEV3d: Design & defend a sustainable energy plan for a location
elements.SEV4a: Effects of human activities on natural resources
elements.SEV4b: Solutions to reduce human impact (smog, ozone, urbanization, ocean acidification)
elements.SEV4c: Human population growth vs. food demand/supply (GMOs, monoculture, desertification, Green Revolution)
elements.SEV5a: Quality of life & human impact (population growth, education, GNP)
elements.SEV5b: Global population patterns (fertility/mortality, demographic transition, pyramids)
elements.SEV5c: Ecological effects of human innovations (Ag, Industrial, Medical, Technological)

items.stem: All of the white-tailed deer living in Red Top Mountain State Park make up which level of biological organization?
options: An organism
A population
A community
An ecosystem

diagnoses.2: Thinks a single-species group is a 'community' rather than a population.

items.stem: Which level of organization includes BOTH the living and the non-living parts of an area?
options: Population
Community
Ecosystem
Organism

diagnoses.1: Believes only the biotic (living) components make up an ecosystem.

items.stem: Every largemouth bass living in one Georgia farm pond represents which level of biological organization?
options: A community
A population
An ecosystem
The biosphere

diagnoses.0: Thinks a single-species group is a 'community' rather than a population.

items.stem: A student says an ecosystem is made of only the living things in an area. What is the student leaving out?
options: Nothing; that definition is complete
The non-living (abiotic) factors such as water, soil, and sunlight
Only the largest animals
The neighboring biosphere

diagnoses.0: Believes only the biotic (living) components make up an ecosystem.

items.stem: A producer level in a food chain contains 10,000 kcal of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the SECONDARY consumers?
options: 1,000 kcal
100 kcal
10 kcal
9,000 kcal

diagnoses.3: Thinks 90% (not 10%) of energy passes to the next trophic level.

items.stem: As energy moves up a food chain, about 90% is not passed to the next level. What happens to that energy?
options: It is destroyed
It is released mostly as heat and is no longer usable by the next level
It is stored permanently in the producers
It travels back to the Sun

diagnoses.0: Believes energy 'lost' between trophic levels is destroyed (violates the 1st Law).

items.stem: Grass in a field stores 50,000 kcal of energy. Following the 10% rule, about how much energy reaches the primary consumers (grasshoppers)?
options: 500 kcal
5,000 kcal
45,000 kcal
50,000 kcal

diagnoses.2: Thinks 90% (not 10%) of energy passes to the next trophic level.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes matter and energy in an ecosystem?
options: Both energy and matter are recycled endlessly
Energy flows one way and is lost as heat, while matter cycles and is reused
Matter flows away as heat while energy is recycled
Both energy and matter are destroyed at each level

diagnoses.0: Believes energy is recycled like matter rather than flowing one way.

items.target: Role of microbes in the nitrogen cycle
items.stem: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas (N₂) directly from the air. What makes nitrogen available to plants?
options: Lightning turns all N₂ into oxygen
Bacteria (microbes) convert N₂ into forms plants can absorb
Plants breathe in N₂ through their leaves
Nitrogen is manufactured inside the plant

diagnoses.2: Thinks plants obtain usable nitrogen by 'breathing it in' rather than through microbial fixation.

items.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stores carbon in living tissue?
options: Cellular respiration
Photosynthesis
Combustion
Decomposition

diagnoses.0: Reverses photosynthesis and respiration in the carbon cycle.

items.stem: Why does phosphorus move differently through its cycle than carbon and nitrogen do?
options: Phosphorus is a gas that stays in the air
Phosphorus rarely enters the atmosphere and is found mostly in rock and soil
Phosphorus is not needed by living things
Phosphorus is found only in the ocean

diagnoses.2: Believes only some cycles matter to life; overlooks phosphorus in DNA, ATP, etc.

items.stem: A student claims the water, carbon, and nitrogen cycles each work completely on their own. Why is this incorrect?
options: It is correct — each cycle is fully separate
The cycles are interconnected; matter moves among them (e.g., decomposers return carbon and nitrogen to soil)
Only the water cycle is real
The cycles interact only inside animals

diagnoses.0: Believes the biogeochemical cycles are completely independent of one another.

items.stem: Desert cacti store water in thick stems and have a waxy coating. These adaptations are mainly a response to which physical factors?
options: High rainfall and cool temperatures
Intense sunlight and scarce water (high insolation, low precipitation)
Cold ocean breezes
Deep, nutrient-rich forest soil

diagnoses.3: Attributes adaptations to biotic/soil factors rather than the controlling abiotic factors.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why organisms living far inland often differ from those living near a coastline?
options: Inland and coastal organisms are always identical
Distance from the ocean changes moisture and temperature, so organisms adapt differently
Coastlines have no effect on organisms
Only the other animals present determine adaptations

diagnoses.3: Believes there is little or no relationship between abiotic factors and adaptations.

items.stem: Rocky Mountain goats have hard, split hooves and are extremely sure-footed. Which physical factor most directly shaped this adaptation?
options: Topography (steep, rocky terrain)
Proximity to the ocean
Length of daylight
Soil nitrogen level

diagnoses.1: Selects an abiotic factor unrelated to the described adaptation.

items.stem: A camel is well adapted to shifting sand and long dry periods but would struggle on steep, rocky cliffs. This shows that:
options: Adaptations depend only on the other animals present
Physical (abiotic) factors strongly influence which adaptations help an organism survive
Adaptations are random and unrelated to the environment
All environments require the same adaptations

diagnoses.0: Believes only biotic factors drive adaptation.
diagnoses.2: Believes adaptations are unrelated to environmental conditions.

items.stem: A healthy Georgia stream usually has dissolved oxygen (DO) between 5 and 8 ppm. Why does dissolved oxygen matter?
options: Fish and other aquatic organisms need it to survive
It makes the water more acidic
Aquatic organisms get all their oxygen from water molecules, so DO does not matter
It increases the turbidity of the water

diagnoses.2: Believes oxygen is unimportant to aquatic life because organisms get it from H₂O molecules.

items.stem: Scientists collect many mayfly, stonefly, and caddisfly larvae (sensitive species) from a stream. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The water is heavily polluted
The water is healthy with enough dissolved oxygen
The water contains no oxygen at all
Nothing can be inferred about water quality

diagnoses.0: Confuses sensitive (pollution-intolerant) species with tolerant, pollution-loving species.

items.stem: Which measurement tells a scientist how cloudy (how much suspended material is in) stream water?
options: pH
Turbidity
Dissolved oxygen
Temperature

diagnoses.0: Confuses acidity/basicity with cloudiness of water.

items.stem: Which macroinvertebrate sample best indicates a HEALTHY Georgia stream?
options: Only tolerant aquatic worms and mosquito larvae
A diverse mix that includes sensitive mayfly and stonefly larvae
No living organisms at all
A huge number of a single tolerant species

diagnoses.3: Equates abundance of one tolerant species with good water quality rather than diversity.

items.target: Volcanism as a short-term climate driver
items.stem: The 1991 eruption of Mt. Pinatubo temporarily lowered Earth's average temperature by about 0.5°C. Why?
options: The volcano added oxygen to the atmosphere
Ash and gases blocked some incoming sunlight
Lava warmed the oceans worldwide
It permanently changed Earth's orbit

diagnoses.3: Confuses a short-term event with long-term orbital (Milankovitch) change.

items.stem: Which is an example of a LONG-term natural cause of climate change (acting over tens of thousands of years)?
options: An El Niño event
A single volcanic eruption
Milankovitch cycles (changes in Earth's orbit and tilt)
A summer heat wave

diagnoses.0: Classifies a short-term (2–7 year) fluctuation as a long-term driver.

items.target: El Niño is a natural, recurring fluctuation
items.stem: During an El Niño event, the trade winds weaken or reverse. El Niño typically occurs:
options: Once every million years
Every 2–7 years, on no fixed schedule
Only because of human air pollution
Every year on the same date

diagnoses.2: Believes all climate change is caused by humans.

items.stem: A student says climates can never change unless humans cause it. Which evidence best corrects this idea?
options: Climates truly never change
Natural events — volcanoes, El Niño, and orbital cycles — changed climate long before humans existed
Only factories can change the climate
Climate change is not real

diagnoses.0: Believes climates cannot change.
diagnoses.2: Believes climate change is always due to human impact.

items.stem: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane affect Earth's temperature by:
options: Blocking all sunlight from entering the atmosphere
Trapping heat near Earth's surface
Cooling the planet by reflecting all heat into space
Producing oxygen for living things

diagnoses.2: Believes greenhouse gases cool the planet rather than trap heat.

items.target: Greenhouse gases are natural and necessary
items.stem: Which statement about greenhouse gases is TRUE?
options: They are entirely human-made and unnatural
They occur naturally and keep Earth warm enough for life
They exist only in the atmosphere and nowhere else
They have no effect on temperature

diagnoses.0: Believes greenhouse gases are not a natural part of Earth's atmosphere.
diagnoses.2: Believes greenhouse gases exist only in the atmosphere (ignores sinks/organisms).

items.stem: Data show that atmospheric CO₂ and average global temperature both rose over the same time period. This pattern is best described as:
options: Evidence that temperature has no pattern
A correlation suggesting rising greenhouse gases and rising temperature are related
Proof that the atmosphere contains no greenhouse gases
Showing no relationship between the two

diagnoses.3: Fails to recognize a correlation between greenhouse gases and temperature.

items.stem: Besides releasing gases, what else can increase the amount of CO₂ in the atmosphere?
options: Planting more forests
Removing carbon sinks such as forests (deforestation), so less CO₂ is absorbed
Increasing the size of the ocean
Nothing else can affect atmospheric CO₂

diagnoses.3: Thinks only emissions — not the loss of sinks — change atmospheric CO₂.

items.stem: Which situation would begin PRIMARY succession?
options: A forest recovering after a wildfire (soil remains)
Bare rock exposed after a glacier retreats (no soil)
An abandoned farm field that still has soil
A flooded meadow that keeps its soil

diagnoses.0: Confuses secondary succession (soil remains) with primary succession.

items.stem: As an ecosystem moves through succession toward a climax community, biomass and biodiversity generally:
options: Increase
Decrease
Stay exactly the same
Disappear completely

diagnoses.2: Believes biodiversity is not part of succession.

items.stem: Lichens and mosses are often the first organisms to colonize bare rock after a disturbance. These are called:
options: Keystone species
Pioneer species
Invasive species
A climax community

diagnoses.3: Confuses the first colonizers with the final, stable climax stage.

items.stem: A student says every climax community looks the same and always takes thousands of years to form. What is the best correction?
options: The student is completely correct
Climax communities differ by biome and can develop over decades up to about 150 years — not always thousands
Succession never reaches a climax community
Deserts and forests reach identical climax communities

diagnoses.0: Believes succession always takes thousands of years and all climax communities are the same.
diagnoses.3: Believes all climax communities look the same regardless of biome.

items.stem: The gopher tortoise digs burrows that many other Georgia species use for shelter and to escape fire. The gopher tortoise is best described as a:
options: Invasive species
Keystone species
Non-native species
Pioneer species

diagnoses.0: Confuses a native species others depend on with a harmful introduced species.

items.stem: Why does higher biodiversity usually make an ecosystem more stable and resilient?
options: It does not — biodiversity has no effect on stability
With more species, others can fill a role if one declines, keeping the ecosystem functioning
More species always cause an ecosystem to collapse
Only the largest species affect stability

diagnoses.0: Believes biodiversity does not make an ecosystem more stable.

items.stem: Kudzu was introduced to the southeastern United States and now grows over and outcompetes native plants. Kudzu is an example of a(n):
options: Endemic species
Keystone species
Invasive species
Indicator species

diagnoses.0: Confuses a spreading introduced species with one found only in a single place.

items.target: Not all non-native species are invasive
items.stem: Which statement about non-native species is correct?
options: Every non-native species becomes invasive
Only some non-native species become invasive; many cause little harm
Non-native species are always helpful to an ecosystem
'Native' and 'non-native' mean the same thing

diagnoses.0: Believes all non-native species end up being invasive species.

items.stem: Which of the following is a NON-renewable energy source?
options: Wind
Solar
Coal
Geothermal

diagnoses.0: Misclassifies a renewable source as non-renewable.

items.target: Why nuclear is grouped as non-renewable
items.stem: Why is nuclear power usually grouped with the non-renewable sources?
options: Because it runs on sunlight
Because it depends on uranium, a limited (non-renewable) fuel
Because it uses flowing water
Because it never produces any waste

diagnoses.0: Believes nuclear power is a renewable energy source.

items.stem: Which list contains ONLY renewable energy sources?
options: Coal, oil, natural gas
Solar, wind, hydropower
Uranium, coal, solar
Natural gas, wind, oil

diagnoses.2: Includes a non-renewable fuel (uranium/coal) among 'renewables'.

items.stem: According to U.S. energy data, which source provided the LARGEST share of U.S. energy in 2021?
options: Solar
Wind
Fossil fuels
Geothermal

diagnoses.0: Assumes all energy sources are used in roughly equal amounts.

items.stem: Which of these is a genuine BENEFIT of solar energy?
options: It works just as well at night as during the day
It is renewable and produces little pollution while generating power
It runs on uranium fuel
It emits large amounts of CO₂ while generating power

diagnoses.0: Overlooks that solar output depends on sunlight/daylight.

items.stem: A student claims renewable energy sources have no drawbacks at all. Which is a REAL drawback of a renewable source?
options: Renewables truly have no drawbacks
Solar and wind depend on weather and daylight and can affect land use and wildlife
They release the most greenhouse gases of any source
They run out quickly, just like fossil fuels

diagnoses.0: Believes renewable energy sources have no risks or drawbacks.

items.stem: Which is a real BENEFIT of fossil fuels compared with many renewable sources?
options: They are renewable
They are reliable and have well-developed infrastructure for storage and transport
They produce no pollution
They can never be depleted

diagnoses.0: Believes fossil fuels are renewable.

items.stem: Which of these is a genuine RISK of nuclear power?
options: It emits large amounts of CO₂ while running
It produces long-lived radioactive waste and can have rare but dangerous malfunctions
It depends entirely on the weather
It has no risks at all

diagnoses.0: Believes nuclear generation emits large amounts of CO₂.

items.stem: Being 'renewable' does NOT automatically make an energy source 'sustainable.' Which example shows this?
options: Sunlight will run out next year
Biofuels can require monoculture farming that depletes soil and uses large amounts of land
Wind is actually non-renewable
Solar panels last forever and use no materials

diagnoses.3: Assumes renewable sources have no material or land costs.

items.stem: To decide whether an energy source is sustainable, scientists should consider:
options: Only how much it costs today
Its full impact from collection to use to disposal, including environmental, economic, and social effects
Only whether it is currently popular
Only how modern the technology looks

diagnoses.0: Believes sustainability only concerns present-day cost/our lifetime.

items.target: Why nuclear is judged not fully sustainable
items.stem: Despite its low emissions, why is nuclear power often judged NOT fully sustainable?
options: Because it produces large amounts of CO₂
Because it creates long-lived radioactive waste and relies on a limited supply of uranium
Because it uses up too much sunlight
Because it is completely harmless

diagnoses.0: Believes nuclear generation is a major CO₂ source.

items.stem: Which question best helps evaluate whether an energy plan is sustainable?
options: Does the technology look modern?
Can it be maintained long-term without seriously damaging the environment, economy, or society?
Is it the cheapest option today, regardless of its effects?
Do most of my friends already use it?

diagnoses.2: Judges sustainability by present cost alone, ignoring long-term effects.

items.target: Account for local conditions in a plan
items.stem: A town in the North Georgia mountains wants to use solar power. Which local challenge must its energy plan address?
options: There is never any sunlight in Georgia
Mountains and trees can block sunlight, so panel placement must be planned carefully
Solar panels only work next to the ocean
Solar power cannot be used anywhere in Georgia

diagnoses.3: Assumes a source that works elsewhere cannot be adapted to local conditions.

items.target: One plan does not fit every location
items.stem: Why won't a single energy plan work for every location in the United States?
options: All locations have exactly the same resources
Available resources and conditions (sun, wind, water, land) differ from place to place
Only coal can be used everywhere
Energy needs are identical everywhere

diagnoses.0: Believes all locations across the U.S. use the same energy resources.

items.target: Weigh trade-offs of a large project
items.stem: Before building a large hydropower dam, planners should carefully consider:
options: Only how tall the dam will look
Cost, effects on biodiversity and fish migration, and flooding of inhabited land
Nothing — large dams have no downsides
Only the color of the reservoir water

diagnoses.2: Believes large renewable projects have no environmental or social costs.

items.target: Features of a good local energy plan
items.stem: A good sustainable energy plan for a specific location is one that:
options: Copies another country's plan exactly
Matches reliable local resources to the area's real needs while limiting environmental and social harm
Uses the most polluting source available
Ignores local geography entirely

diagnoses.0: Assumes a plan can simply be copied without regard to local conditions.

items.stem: When excess nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer runs off farms into a lake, it often causes:
options: Clearer, healthier water
Algal blooms that lower dissolved oxygen and harm aquatic life (eutrophication)
An increase in oxygen for fish
No change at all to the water

diagnoses.2: Thinks nutrient runoff raises dissolved oxygen instead of depleting it.

items.stem: A student says human activities do not really affect natural resources. Which example best refutes this claim?
options: Human activities have no measurable effect
Mining can cause erosion and contaminate groundwater
Only volcanoes affect natural resources
Natural resources are unlimited

diagnoses.0: Believes human activities do not impact natural resources.
diagnoses.3: Believes natural resources are effectively unlimited.

items.stem: Nitrogen fertilizer from Midwest farms travels down the Mississippi River and helps create a low-oxygen 'dead zone' in the Gulf of Mexico. This is an example of:
options: A natural process unrelated to humans
How farming runoff can harm an aquatic ecosystem far downstream
An improvement in Gulf water quality
Something that only affects the farm's own soil

diagnoses.3: Believes a human activity only affects its immediate location.

items.stem: Which pairing of a human activity and its impact is correct?
options: Urbanization → cleaner rivers
Urbanization → more paved surfaces and runoff that carry pollutants into waterways
Overfishing → larger fish populations
Deforestation → less erosion

diagnoses.0: Believes only some, obvious human activities affect resources.

items.stem: Ocean acidification happens as the ocean absorbs excess CO₂, forming carbonic acid. Which statement is accurate?
options: The ocean has literally turned into acid
Ocean pH is dropping (becoming less basic), which harms shell-forming organisms
CO₂ has no effect on ocean chemistry
The ocean is becoming more basic

diagnoses.0: Believes ocean acidification means the ocean has become an acid.

items.stem: Adding rooftop gardens and green spaces in a city most directly helps reduce:
options: The urban heat island effect
Ocean tides
Volcanic eruptions
Earth's orbital tilt

diagnoses.1: Applies a local urban solution to an unrelated global/geologic process.

items.stem: Which action most directly reduces photochemical smog?
options: Banning rooftop gardens
Reducing emissions from vehicles and power plants
Increasing overall fossil-fuel use
Removing all trees from cities

diagnoses.2: Selects an action that increases the pollutants causing smog.

items.stem: A student says nothing can be done to reduce human impact on the environment. Which real example refutes this?
options: Nothing humans have tried has ever worked
Banning certain ozone-depleting chemicals (like CFCs) helped the ozone layer begin to recover
Using more ozone-depleting chemicals helps
Removing green spaces from cities

diagnoses.0: Believes no solutions will work to reduce human impact.

items.stem: Growing the same crop on the same land year after year (monoculture) can lead to:
options: Richer soil over time
Depleted soil nutrients and, over time, possible desertification
Permanently high yields with no added inputs
Greater biodiversity in the soil

diagnoses.0: Believes repeated monoculture improves soil rather than depleting it.
diagnoses.2: Believes it is easy to keep increasing food supply indefinitely.

items.stem: The Green Revolution greatly increased grain yields worldwide. What is a major TRADE-OFF of these high-yield crops?
options: They require no water
They require large amounts of fertilizer and pesticides
They remove the need for farming altogether
They out-produce native strains in every environment with no inputs

diagnoses.3: Believes high-yield strains always outperform native strains without added inputs.

items.stem: What is one purpose of genetically modified (GMO) crops?
options: To make crops less nutritious
To improve traits such as pest resistance, drought tolerance, or nutrition
To guarantee that crops need no soil to grow
To deliberately reduce the food supply

diagnoses.0: Holds a purely negative misunderstanding of what GMOs are designed to do.

items.stem: Why do many farmers use crop rotation instead of continuous monoculture?
options: To deplete the soil faster
Because different crops use and replenish different nutrients, helping protect the soil
Because all plants need exactly the same nutrients
To intentionally cause desertification

diagnoses.2: Believes all crops draw the same nutrients, so rotation would make no difference.

items.stem: Compared with Less Developed Countries (LDCs), More Developed Countries (MDCs) generally have:
options: Lower income and higher fertility rates
Higher income (GNP) and lower total fertility rates
Identical income and fertility rates
No formal education systems

diagnoses.0: Reverses the relationship between development, income, and fertility.

items.target: Education affects fertility & quality of life
items.stem: Research shows that increasing access to education, especially for women, tends to:
options: Sharply raise fertility rates
Lower fertility rates and improve quality of life
Have no effect on population or quality of life
Instantly eliminate all environmental impact

diagnoses.2: Believes education does not affect quality of life or population growth.

items.stem: The replacement fertility rate for humans is about 2.1 births per woman. A total fertility rate well ABOVE 2.1 suggests that a population is:
options: Shrinking
Growing
Perfectly stable
Producing no children

diagnoses.0: Misreads a high fertility rate as causing population decline.

items.target: Development is linked to human impact
items.stem: Which statement about a nation's development and its impact on the environment is best supported?
options: A nation's development has no connection to its environmental impact
Development level is connected to both quality of life and environmental impact
Only LDCs affect the environment
Only MDCs affect the environment

diagnoses.0: Believes the development of a nation does not affect its impact on Earth.

items.stem: A population increases in size when:
options: The death rate is greater than the birth rate
The birth (fertility) rate is greater than the death (mortality) rate
Birth and death rates are exactly equal
No individuals are born

diagnoses.0: Reverses the relationship between birth rate, death rate, and growth.

items.stem: A population pyramid shaped like a wide-based triangle usually indicates a country with:
options: Low fertility and long life expectancy
A high fertility rate with many young people
A shrinking population made up mostly of elderly people
An equal number at every age, with no pattern

diagnoses.2: Misinterprets a wide base (many young) as an aging, shrinking population.

items.stem: A student claims that all populations on Earth are growing at the same rate. Why is this incorrect?
options: It is correct — growth is identical everywhere
Growth is uneven; different countries have different fertility and mortality rates
No populations anywhere are growing
Only the U.S. population ever changes

diagnoses.0: Believes all populations across the world grow at the same rate.

items.stem: A population pyramid shaped like a tall 'rocket' (fairly even width top to bottom) most likely represents a country with:
options: Very high fertility and almost no elderly people
A low fertility rate near replacement, with both young and old present
No older people at all
Only children and no adults

diagnoses.0: Confuses the even 'rocket' shape (low fertility) with a wide-based high-fertility pyramid.

items.stem: The factories of the Industrial Revolution greatly increased demand for which resource, adding pollution to the air?
options: Wind only
Coal and other fossil fuels
Sunlight
None — factories used no energy

diagnoses.3: Overlooks the enormous fossil-fuel demand created by industrialization.

items.stem: Advances in medicine (vaccines, surgery, disease control) affected human populations mainly by:
options: Decreasing human life expectancy
Increasing life expectancy and contributing to population growth
Having no effect on population size
Reducing the total human population

diagnoses.2: Believes technological/medical innovations do not affect population or impact.

items.stem: Agricultural innovations such as tractors and chemical fertilizers allowed:
options: Far less food to be grown
More food to be grown with fewer workers, but with more fuel and land use
Farming to stop almost entirely
Food production with no environmental effects

diagnoses.3: Believes new technologies carry no environmental cost.

items.stem: A student says new technologies never increase human impact on the environment. Which example best refutes this?
options: Technology has no environmental cost of any kind
Engines and factories increased fossil-fuel use, mining, and pollution
Technology only ever helps and never harms
Innovations always reduce resource use to zero

diagnoses.0: Believes new technologies do not increase human impact.

items.stem: Which individual action would most reduce a person's environmental impact?
options: Leaving lights and devices on all day
Biking or taking public transportation instead of driving alone
Buying more single-use plastic products
Throwing away items that could be reused

diagnoses.0: Selects an action that increases, rather than reduces, energy use.

items.stem: A student says one person's choices cannot make any difference. Which idea best challenges this?
options: One person truly cannot matter
Small actions add up across many people to create large impacts
Only governments can affect the environment
Recycling never helps anything

diagnoses.0: Believes one person cannot make a difference.
diagnoses.2: Places all responsibility on governments, dismissing individual choices.

items.stem: How can market forces affect a person's ability to make sustainable choices?
options: Market options and prices have no effect on people's choices
The available options and their prices (for example, plastic vs. cardboard packaging) shape what people can realistically buy
Every product is always available plastic-free and free of charge
Cost never influences a purchase decision

diagnoses.0: Overlooks how market forces and cost constrain personal choices.

items.stem: Plastics that are thrown away improperly often end up as:
options: Clean drinking water
Microplastics in oceans, waterways, and even food
Useful nutrients that enrich the soil
Harmless gases that leave no trace

diagnoses.2: Believes discarded plastics harmlessly break down into soil nutrients.
